technical_and_design_decisions: Use JUnit 5 as the testing framework, aligned with the project's existing test stack
Leverage Spring's built-in test support (e.g., @SpringBootTest, @MockBean) to minimize boilerplate code for module tests
Use Mockito for mocking external service dependencies (HDFS cluster, SMTP mail server) to ensure tests are fast, reliable, and do not require external infrastructure
Structure all new acceptance tests following the project's existing test package and naming conventions to ensure consistency with existing test suites
Develop reusable common test utilities (test data generators, assertion helpers, mock configuration) shared across all module test suites to reduce duplication and maintenance overhead
Configure new tests to run as part of the existing project build lifecycle so they are automatically included in CI builds without modifying build tool configuration
assumptions: The existing CI pipeline (e.g., Jenkins, GitHub Actions) is already configured to run the project's test suite, and only requires adding the new test classes to the existing test source set to include them in CI builds
All target modules have stable, well-documented public APIs with no breaking changes expected during the test development period

Required test dependencies for mocking external services (e.g., hdfs-minidcluster, mock mail server libraries) are already available in the project's dependency management system, with no need for new dependency approval processes
Existing functional test cases or module specification documents are available to serve as a basis for defining acceptance test scenarios, eliminating the need for reverse-engineering module behavior
The development environment is pre-configured with JDK 17+, the project's build tool (Maven/Gradle), and all required testing frameworks, with no additional environment setup needed
No changes to the target modules' source code are required to support the acceptance tests (i.e., tests will use existing public APIs only)
